questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+3\,j-j) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}\cdot 2-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (1+2t)}{2})\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{e}^{2t}-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t))dt \\  & ={[{e}^{2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{e}^{2(1)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (1))]-[{e}^{2(0)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (0))] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})]-[1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+0]-[1+0] \\  & ={e}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-8{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(-1,0)$ to the point $N(2,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i$ and $b=2\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =-i+t(2\,i+4\,j-(-i)) \\  & =-i+t(3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =(3t-1)\,i+4t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=3t-1$ and $y(t)=4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=3\,i+4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t(3)-(3t-1)(4)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\,dt \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=2\sqrt{x}$ traversed from the point $P(1,2)$ to point $Q(4,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=2\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-2t)\cdot 2t+({t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}t({t}^{2}-2t)+({t}^{2}+2t)\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & =2{[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2[(\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}+{2}^{2})-(\frac{{1}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}+{1}^{2})] \\  & =2[4-\frac{8}{3}+4-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3}-1] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{53}{12} \\  & =\frac{53}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(-1,0)$ to the point $(0,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+9\pi )-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +6\pi ) \\  & =(0+9\pi )-(-1+6\pi ) \\  & =3\pi +1\end{aligned}
$$
